questions.question: Trace 100 units of insolation from the sun to the surface and back out again, and explain why the earth's heat budget balances globally but not at every latitude.
questions.expected_answer: Of 100 units of incoming short-wave solar radiation, about 30 are reflected straight back to space by cloud tops, dust and bright surfaces such as snow and pale desert soils — that reflected proportion is the albedo. About 20 units are absorbed on the way through by ozone, water vapour, dust and cloud, leaving roughly 50 units to be absorbed at the earth's surface. The surface warms and re-radiates that energy upward as long-wave terrestrial radiation, which the atmosphere absorbs very effectively. Over a year the planet as a whole loses to space exactly as much energy as it receives, otherwise it would heat or cool without limit. But the balance holds only for the total: between roughly 40 degrees north and 40 degrees south there is a permanent energy surplus, and poleward of those latitudes a permanent deficit. That imbalance is corrected by transfer rather than radiation — winds moving warm air poleward and ocean currents such as the Agulhas doing the same in water. Global circulation therefore exists to settle an energy debt.

questions.question: Explain the greenhouse effect step by step, and distinguish the natural greenhouse effect from the enhanced greenhouse effect.
questions.expected_answer: Short-wave solar radiation passes through the atmosphere with little absorption and is absorbed by the earth's surface, which warms. The surface re-radiates that energy as long-wave terrestrial radiation. Greenhouse gases — water vapour, carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide, ozone and CFCs — absorb this long-wave radiation and re-radiate it in all directions, including back down to the surface as counter-radiation, so the lower atmosphere is warmer than it would otherwise be. This natural process is essential: without it the global average surface temperature would be about −18 °C instead of roughly 15 °C. The enhanced greenhouse effect is the human intensification of it, as burning fossil fuels, deforestation, livestock and rice agriculture, landfills and cement manufacture add greenhouse gases faster than natural sinks remove them. The examiner's key distinction is that the natural effect makes the planet habitable while the enhanced effect, which we caused, is warming it further.

questions.question: Compare Durban and Upington, using at least four of the temperature factors, and explain why the annual temperature range differs so sharply between them.
questions.expected_answer: Latitude is similar for both, so it does not explain the difference; the other factors do. Distance from the sea is decisive: Durban is coastal, and water heats and cools far more slowly than land because it is transparent, mixes by waves and currents, loses heat to evaporation and needs more energy per degree — so the sea moderates Durban's temperatures and gives it a small annual range. Upington lies deep in the interior with no such moderating influence, so it swings from very hot summers to cold winter nights: a large annual range. Ocean currents reinforce this: the warm Agulhas Current flows south past Durban, keeping the air above it warm and supplying moisture for humidity and summer rain. Cloud cover matters too, since Durban's greater humidity and cloudiness lower its daytime maxima and raise its night minima, while Upington's clear skies allow strong daytime heating and rapid night-time radiation loss. Altitude plays a smaller role here, but Upington's inland plateau position adds to the contrast in daily range.
